To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) the wide-band ambiguity and the Wigner-Ville distributions are related by an integral transform that is the inverse of the transform relating the narrow-band ambiguity to the Wigner-Vile distribution, and that (2) a spectrogram constructed with a family of constant-Q or proportional-bandwidth filters can be obtained from the Q distribution by a convolution-like operator or by forming a wide-band cross- ambiguity function.

the Q distributions, a wide-band generalization of the Wigner-Ville distribution, can be obtained from a convolution-like operation between two Q distributions or from the magnitude-squared of a wide-band ambiguity function.

developing new techniques for the analysis and synthesis of wide-band signals.
the development of a new class of time-frequency representations that can be used for the analysis of nonstationary signals.
the development of wideband time-frequency representations for signal analysis and processing.

the Wigner-Ville distribution and its wide-band extension, the Q distribution, provide a powerful set of tools for the analysis of wide-band signals and scattering functions.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the Wigner-Ville distribution is a highly accurate estimate for instantaneous frequency.

we have shown that there are two types of time-frequency distributions: narrowband and wideband, and that the wideband distributions are more useful than the narrowband for the analysis of wideband signals.

the Wigner-Ville distribution is the best time-frequency representation of a signal for the case of constant bandwidth filters, while the Q distribution is the best for the case of proportional bandwidth filters.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the Q distribution is a natural wide-band extension of the Wigner-Ville distribution and that it may be useful in a variety of problems in radar, sonar, and communications.
